Merab
MEE-rab
n. (proper, elder daughter of Saul; Hebrew, increase)
Hebrew Merab, from rabah, to increase — increase, or multiplication. She was Saul's firstborn daughter, offered to David as a snare and then given to another man.

Biblical Definition

The family of Saul is set out plainly: “Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchishua: and the names of his two daughters were these; the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal” (1 Samuel 14:49). Then the offer, and the narrator's exposure of the motive behind it: “And Saul said to David, Behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife: only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles. For Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him” (1 Samuel 18:17). Pious language — fight the LORD'S battles — concealing an attempt at murder by proxy. And then the promise was simply broken: “But it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul's daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife” (1 Samuel 18:19). Merab is never recorded as speaking. She is offered, withdrawn and disposed of, and her five sons were afterwards hanged before the LORD in Gibeon.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of the elder daughter of Saul, promised to David and given to Adriel the Meholathite.

BETROTH, v.t. To contract to any one, in order to a future marriage; to promise or pledge one to be the future spouse of another.

PLEDGE, n. Something put in pawn; a warrant; a security; that which is deposited as security for the performance of an act.

SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals; anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble unexpectedly.

DOWRY, n. The money, goods or estate which a woman brings to her husband in marriage; or a gift given by the husband for the wife.

PRETEXT, n. Pretence; false appearance; ostensible reason or motive assigned or assumed as a color or cover.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 14:49 — "Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchishua: and the names of his two daughters were these; the name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal:"

1 Samuel 18:17 — "And Saul said to David, Behold my elder daughter Merab, her will I give thee to wife: only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles. For Saul said, Let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him."

1 Samuel 18:19 — "But it came to pass at the time when Merab Saul's daughter should have been given to David, that she was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife."

2 Samuel 21:8 — "But the king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bare unto Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite:"

Modern Corruption

Marriage is now negotiated as a private arrangement between two adults, and Scripture's exposure of Merab's treatment goes unread — a father who used his daughter as bait and broke his word without a word from her.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the name. The live matter is the honesty of the narrative, which is easily missed because Merab is given no dialogue. Saul offers her with a spiritual exhortation attached — only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles — and the historian tells us in the next clause what Saul was actually thinking: let not mine hand be upon him, but let the hand of the Philistines be upon him. Scripture refuses to let religious language cover the intent underneath it, and it exposes the king rather than the shepherd.

The second thing the passage establishes is that a daughter is not a counter to be played. Merab is promised and then handed to Adriel the Meholathite with no explanation, and David is left to face the shame of a broken betrothal. A father's authority over a household is real in Scripture and it is never absolute; it is held under God, for the good of those under it, and Saul's use of it here is set down as part of the record of a man the Spirit of the LORD had departed from. The record's sympathy is with the ones who had no voice in it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Merab (H4764), increase; rabah (H7235), to multiply; bekowrah (H1062), birthright or the firstborn's place; mowqesh (H4170), a snare.

expand to see more

Hebrew Merab (H4764) — Merab, increase; Saul's firstborn daughter.

Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to become many, to increase; the root of her name.

Hebrew bekowrah (H1062) — the right of the firstborn; hers by birth, hers in name only.

Hebrew mowqesh (H4170) — a snare, a bait; what Saul intended Michal to be for David.

Hebrew Miykal (H4324) — Michal, her younger sister, given in her place.

Usage

"“The name of the firstborn Merab, and the name of the younger Michal”."

"“Only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD'S battles” — a pious snare."

"“She was given unto Adriel the Meholathite to wife” — the promise broken."
